No MPs or ministers on private bank boards: Govt plans sweeping reforms
item.description:
The government is set to restrict ministers, members of parliament (MPs) and local government representatives from serving on the boards of private banks.

Other proposed changes include reducing the dominance of members of the same family on bank boards, increasing the number of independent directors and cutting the maximum consecutive tenure of directors from 12 years to six. The changes are being introduced to restore good governance in the banking sector and protect depositors’ interests.

The Financial Institutions Division of the Ministry of Finance has finalised a draft amendment to the Bank Company Act, 1991. It proposes several significant changes, including measures to reduce political influence over bank boards.

Most of the recommendations made jointly by the Financial Institutions Division and Bangladesh Bank during the interim government’s tenure to amend the law have been retained in the latest draft. Relevant sources said the draft would be sent to the Cabinet Division this week. It would then be placed before a Cabinet meeting for approval.

Welcoming the initiative, Bangladesh Association of Banks (BAB) Chairman Abdul Hai Sarker told Prothom Alo, “I believe it is better for political figures to stay away from bank boards.”

Under the draft, Cabinet members or persons of equivalent status, MPs and local government representatives will not be eligible to serve as bank directors. Political office-holders will also be disqualified from being appointed managing directors or chief executive officers of banks. The proposals are intended to discourage political interference in the management of banks.

The existing law contains no explicit prohibition on ministers and MPs serving on bank boards. However, ministers are subject to the restrictions set out in Article 147 of the Constitution.

Sub-article (3) of the article states that no member of the Cabinet may hold an office of profit or participate in the management or direction of any company, association or institution operated for profit or gain.

Welcoming the initiative, Bangladesh Association of Banks (BAB) Chairman Abdul Hai Sarker told Prothom Alo, “I believe it is better for political figures to stay away from bank boards.”

Maximum three from a family allowed in bank boards

Two directors from same family

To reduce the dominance of members of the same family on bank boards, a proposal has been made to limit their number. Currently, up to three members of a single family can serve as directors of the same bank at the same time. The new proposal seeks to reduce this number to two.

It also proposes reducing the number of representative directors from institutions connected to or controlled by the same family from two to one.

During the Awami League government’s tenure, several business groups, including S Alam Group, Beximco, Premier Group and Sikder Group, faced allegations of taking control of banks and financial institutions and engaging in widespread irregularities and corruption.

Influential figures from these groups placed not only themselves but also their wives or husbands, sons and daughters, sons-in-law and close relatives on bank boards. The BAB believes the new proposals are intended to reduce control of families over bank boards.

The limit was originally six years. An amendment in 2018 increased it to nine years, and it was extended further to 12 years in 2023. The latest proposal seeks to bring it back to six years.

Directors’ consecutive tenure to be six years

A proposal has been made to reduce the maximum consecutive tenure of bank directors from 12 years to six years. The limit was originally six years. An amendment in 2018 increased it to nine years, and it was extended further to 12 years in 2023.

The latest proposal seeks to bring it back to six years. It states that after serving six consecutive years, a director will not be eligible to serve on the board of the same bank for the following three years.

When asked about the proposal, the chairman of the Bangladesh Association of Banks (BAB) said, “We had proposed nine years. A decision has been made to set it at six years. We have accepted it.”

One more independent director

The number of independent directors on bank boards will increase. At present, a board can have up to 20 members, including two to three independent directors. The proposal seeks to increase this number to three to four.

For boards with fewer than 20 members, the current requirement is to have at least two independent directors. The proposal would raise that number to three.

The proposal also seeks to clarify that the appointment of independent directors must be free from the influence of the bank’s management and shareholders. A provision is proposed to disqualify anyone with past, present or future interests connected to the bank from being considered an independent director.

S Alam went to Arastoo’s home and told him, “you have to step down”

Concessions for strategic investors

A proposal has been made to relax the shareholding limit to attract strategic investors to bank ownership. At present, no individual, institution or members of the same family can directly or indirectly purchase more than 10 per cent of a bank’s shares.

Under the new proposal, Bangladesh Bank would be empowered to relax this limit for strategic investors, taking the interests of the banking sector into account.

The central bank will determine the qualifications, suitability criteria and conditions for such investors. While the 10 per cent limit would remain in place for ordinary investors, special investors would be given an opportunity to benefit from an exception.

BAB Chairman Abdul Hai Sarker said, “We had demanded that no discrimination be created by offering greater benefits to foreigners and fewer to local investors.”

The proposal also seeks to increase the central bank’s control over changes to a bank’s articles of association, which set out its fundamental rules and governance arrangements.

Loans must be repaid even after leaving office

The draft amendment to the Bank Company Act also proposes stricter provisions on the repayment of loans taken while serving as a bank director. Under the current law, if a director’s position becomes vacant, the bank can recover money owed by the director by adjusting it against their shares.

The new proposal states that after a director leaves office, they must repay the full outstanding amount of any advances or loans taken from the bank concerned. There will be no scope to regularise the loan through rescheduling or any other means.

A new provision is also being introduced to ensure directors attend board meetings. A director will not be allowed to remain absent from meetings for more than three consecutive months. However, permission to remain absent for longer than this period may be granted no more than once a year.

World Bank report: Growth weakens, poverty rises, banking sector at risk

Bangladesh Bank’s controls to be expanded

If a bank’s board of directors takes actions contrary to depositors’ interests, Bangladesh Bank can dissolve the board. Under the new proposal, the central bank will be able to reconstitute the board as it sees fit. It will also be able to shorten or extend the board’s tenure as necessary, although the term cannot exceed three years.

The proposal also includes a provision for directors to be elected by the bank’s members at the next annual general meeting after the formation of a new board. Bangladesh Bank will be able to issue the necessary directives in this regard.

The proposal also seeks to increase the central bank’s control over changes to a bank’s articles of association, which set out its fundamental rules and governance arrangements. No application to amend a bank company’s articles of association will be accepted without a no-objection certificate from Bangladesh Bank.

In addition, a proposal has been made to treat any organisation as an entity connected to a person’s interests if that person serves as one of its directors, owns more than 20 per cent of its shares or acts as a guarantor for its loans.

At present, failure to provide required accounts, statements or information, or violation of an order issued by Bangladesh Bank, is punishable by a fine of Tk 20,000 to Tk 500,000. Under the new proposal, the minimum fine will be increased to Tk 50,000, while the maximum will remain unchanged at Tk 500,000.

Former Bangladesh Bank governor Ahsan H Mansur believes that crucial laws, including the Bangladesh Bank Order and the Distressed Asset Management Act, must also be passed by parliament to reform the banking sector.

Former governor welcomes move

Former Bangladesh Bank governor Ahsan H Mansur has described the initiative to amend the Bank Company Act as positive. However, he believes further changes are needed in several areas.

Ahsan Mansur told Prothom Alo that the proportion of independent directors should be increased to 50 per cent, as this is the global practice. He also said more opportunities should be created for strategic investors.

Both foreign and local institutional investors could be allowed to purchase up to 20, 30 or even 100 per cent of a bank’s shares. However, he said, this opportunity should be available to institutions, not individuals.

Ahsan H Mansur said that, during his tenure as governor, he had proposed limiting directors’ consecutive tenure to six years and allowing no more than two directors from the same family.

He added that, alongside ministers and members of parliament, former senior government officials and judges should also not be appointed to bank boards. He believes that crucial laws, including the Bangladesh Bank Order and the Distressed Asset Management Act, must also be passed by parliament to reform the banking sector.

item.title: NCP to meet PM tomorrow, 4 leaders including Nahid Islam to attend
item.description:
The National Citizen Party (NCP) has welcomed Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s call for national unity amid sabotage surrounding programmes announced by Awami League (activities banned in the country).

Responding to the prime minister’s invitation for dialogue, an NCP delegation will meet him at tomorrow afternoon, on Monday.

The four-member delegation will be led by NCP Convener and Chief Whip of the opposition in parliament Nahid Islam.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has initiated talks with anti-fascist political parties that took part in the July mass uprising. The dialogue is set to begin with tomorrow’s meeting with the NCP, followed by talks with Jamaat-e-Islami and other political parties.

Nahid Islam, who is currently visiting the United Kingdom, is scheduled to return this afternoon, on Sunday. The names of the other members of the delegation will be finalised in consultation with him after his return, NCP sources said.

Sarwar Tushar, a joint convener of the party and a member of its highest policymaking body, the Political Council, said in a statement sent to the media late Saturday night that an NCP delegation will meet the prime minister on 23 November at his invitation.

The statement said the NCP views the prime minister’s invitation positively. It also said the party believes national unity must be based on implementing the verdict of the referendum, bringing the Awami League to justice as a fascist and terrorist organisation, and prosecuting the July massacre.

Relevant sources said the ruling BNP and the Prime Minister’s Office have already begun preparations to organise the dialogue.

item.title: Chicago proposes naming street after Khaleda Zia
item.description:
A proposal has been put forward to name a street in Chicago, US, after former Bangladesh prime minister and late BNP chairperson Khaleda Zia, with the honorary name “Honorary Mother of Democracy Begum Khaleda Zia Way”, according to the Chicago City Council.
The proposal, dated September 23, 2026, was submitted by the Chicago City Council’s Committee on Transportation and Public Way. It seeks to designate a section of the eastern side of Upper Wacker Drive, stretching from West Jackson Boulevard to West Adams Street near Willis Tower, in Khaleda Zia’s honour.
The proposal describes Khaleda Zia as a prominent Bangladeshi stateswoman who served as prime minister for two terms, from 1991 to 1996 and from 2001 to 2006.
As Bangladesh’s first female prime minister, she dedicated decades to public service and played a historic role in the movement to restore parliamentary democracy in the country, it says.
It also notes that she became known as the “Mother of Democracy” for her commitment to democratic governance, constitutional institutions and people's political rights.
The proposal highlights her contributions to expanding educational opportunities for girls, particularly her policy of providing free education to girls up to the 12th grade.
It states that Khaleda Zia died on December 30, 2025, leaving behind a legacy of democratic leadership, public service and dedication to the country.
It also refers to her family and the next generation of political leadership in Bangladesh, specifically mentioning her son, Tarique Rahman.
The proposal further cites Chicago’s Willis Tower, formerly known as the Sears Tower, as a symbol of the city's architectural and engineering achievements. It highlights the contributions of Bangladeshi-American engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan to Chicago's skyline.
If approved by the Chicago City Council and officially published, the proposal will take effect, with the city's commissioner of transportation directed to take the necessary steps to implement the honorary street naming.

item.title: Dhaka says Indian outlets misreported PM's remarks
item.description:
Bangladesh on Sunday disputed reports by some Indian media outlets that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman blamed India for violence attributed to the activity-banned Awami League, saying he named no country in his November 19 speech in Lalmonirhat.
While responding to a question about the accuracy of the reports, a Foreign Ministry spokesperson told BSS that those Indian outlets had misreported the prime minister's remarks.
"The speech was misreported by these (Indian) media since he (Prime Minister Tarique Rahman) did not mention any country by name," said the spokesperson.
"The Awami fascist terrorists are running amok in different continents. The entire world has witnessed the serious violence they have inflicted on innocent people," he added.
The spokesperson alleged that the violence was creating security problems in several countries, damaging Bangladesh's standing abroad and harming the reputation of Bangladeshi expatriate communities.
The spokesperson called on countries to act to prevent the violence from spreading.

item.title: Shama Obaed: Unrest in garment sector politically motivated
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam has described the ongoing unrest in the country’s ready-made garment (RMG) sector as politically motivated.
She made the remarks at a conference on occupational health and safety (OSH) in the workplace at Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel in Dhaka on Sunday.
She said the unrest was being fuelled on the streets with the intention of harming the country’s economy, future and garment industry.
Shama Obaed said the government was committed to addressing workers’ legitimate demands and supporting the growth of the RMG sector.
Noting that the current fiscal year’s budget was worker-friendly and supportive of the garment industry, she said the ongoing activities suggested that those behind the unrest wanted to damage Bangladesh’s economy and garment sector. She also alleged that they sought to undermine the progress in women’s empowerment made through the industry and push Bangladesh towards dysfunction.
She said protecting the sector was not solely the responsibility of the government, workers or garment owners, but a collective duty. She urged all stakeholders, including the international community, to work together to end the unrest.
Reflecting on the industry’s development, she said garments produced in Gazipur now reach markets in Stockholm, Amsterdam, Copenhagen and Toronto. She recalled that the vision of promoting “Made in Bangladesh” globally was first conceived by the late president Ziaur Rahman in the early 1980s and later advanced through policy support from former prime minister Khaleda Zia. She said the BNP government had worked to expand the industry while ensuring workers’ safety and labour rights.
Citing figures on exports and migration, Shama Obaed said more than 15 million Bangladeshis were employed in 176 countries worldwide. In the last fiscal year, the European Union imported garments worth around $19 billion from Bangladesh, while the United States imported garments worth approximately $7.7 billion.
She said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs was working through diplomatic missions and multilateral forums to protect migrant workers’ rights and promote safe, orderly and regular migration.
She also thanked development partners, including the EU, Denmark, the Netherlands, Sweden, Canada and the International Labour Organization (ILO), for their support. She said the UN General Assembly’s decision last October to extend Bangladesh’s preparatory period for graduation from least developed country (LDC) status by three years reflected the international community’s confidence in the country.
Emphasizing the importance of research, she said policies provided direction while research laid the necessary foundation. Reliable national data, she added, strengthened Bangladesh’s position in international negotiations on trade concessions, market access and investment.
She expressed hope that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare would continue working closely with development partners.
In her concluding remarks, Shama Obaed said a nation’s true wealth was measured not by its towering structures but by the health, safety and dignity of the people who built them.
She called for a safe and equitable Bangladesh guided by research and evidence, where no worker would have to risk their life or health simply to earn a living.

Security stepped up along border to prevent entry of ‘controversial’ persons
item.description:
Border security has been strengthened to prevent any controversial individuals from entering Bangladesh in December, said Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) Director General Major General Mohammad Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui.

He made the remarks in response to a question from journalists after inspecting the Akhaura International Immigration Checkpost in Brahmanbaria on Sunday afternoon.

Earlier, he arrived by helicopter at the Hirapur School playground in Akhaura at around 3:30 pm.

BGB Director General Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui said it was the responsibility of the BGB to guard the country’s entire border. Its duties included preventing smuggling and ensuring that no one could travel illegally across the border in either direction.

“As part of that responsibility, border security has been strengthened, particularly during this month of December, to prevent any illegal individuals or controversial figures from entering Bangladesh, while also preventing anyone from leaving the country illegally. We also want to prevent push-ins, drug smuggling, and the entry of weapons and explosives,” he said.

Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui said, “That is why I am inspecting the border areas of Feni, Cumilla and Akhaura today. We have strengthened our security arrangements to ensure that these objectives are met. We must implement the government’s directives and fulfil the expectations of the country and its people. I have come here today to inspect the situation on the ground and ensure that border security is maintained to the fullest extent possible.”

Seeking cooperation from local residents, the BGB chief said, “Those of you who live in the area often have access to a great deal of information. If you learn of anyone planning to enter or leave the country, please inform us. If you share such information with the BGB, we will take appropriate measures to prevent it, Insha’Allah.”

BGB Regional Commander Brigadier General Saiful Islam, Sarail Sector Commander Colonel Rakib Hasan, 25 BGB Battalion Commander Lieutenant Colonel Jabbar Ahmed and other relevant officials were present during the visit.

item.title: COP31 fails to agree climate deal in chaotic finale
item.description:
TURKEY-AUSTRALIA-UN-CLIMATE-COP31

The COP31 climate talks headed for a historic defeat Sunday after the EU and other countries refused to endorse a pact that omitted fossil fuels as the summit lurched into record overtime in Turkey.

The main deal was rejected by a host of nations 44 hours after the summit’s official close in a chaotic COP31 finale in the Turkish city of Antalya.

“We will not endorse a cover decision... that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change,” said Ireland’s climate minister, Darragh O’Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency.

COP31 President Murat Kurum conceded the deal had failed to reach consensus.

“I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted,” he told the closing session.

Fossil fuels are a flashpoint at the climate talks, which come against a difficult backdrop of soaring energy prices and geopolitical tensions stemming from the war between the United States and Iran that has roiled the Middle East.

Language around fossil fuels is fiercely opposed by petrostates such as Saudi Arabia.

With expectations low, negotiations chief Australia had sought an overarching “cover decision” to capture what countries agreed at COP31 and send a signal about the future course of climate action.

But the final proposal failed to mention coal, oil and gas at all, plunging the summit into turmoil as it broke the record for the longest-ever UN climate conference.

“We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future,” the Marshall Islands climate envoy Kathy Jetnil-Kijiner told delegates.

Panama, a vocal critic of the UN climate talks, Vanuatu and Belize also rejected the pact.

Outside the assembly hall, O’Brien told AFP the summit had been “hijacked by some oil states”.

Decisions at the UN climate talks are taken by consensus, meaning just one of the nearly 200 nations involved can block agreement.

‘Licence to keep polluting’

Threats of a walkout Saturday prompted Turkey and Australia to convene a hurried meeting between the European Union and Saudi Arabia but a compromise remained elusive.

The latest text introduces an oblique reference to a previous global deal in 2023 to shift the world away from fossil fuels but stops short of naming them explicitly.

The text also proposed retaining a push to expand carbon capture, a technology championed by the fossil fuel industry but criticised as costly and ineffective in cutting emissions.

“We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table and that countries select from these solutions depending on their national circumstances,” said Saudi climate negotiator Mohammad Ayoub, who spoke on behalf of the wider Arab Group of nations.

Climate campaigners had urged countries to reject the deal.

“This text isn’t a climate plan. It’s a licence to keep polluting,” said Sara Shaw of environmental group 350.org.

The summit had been under pressure to show progress on tackling soaring greenhouse gas emissions in a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal and Indonesia.

Facing blowback over fossil fuels, Turkey and Australia pointed to “electrification” as a way to cut heat-trapping emissions and bolster energy security.

This works by replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels directly -- like diesel cars and gas heating -- with electric alternatives.

‘Profound disappointment’

The draft calls for global efforts to boost the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 and the expansion of “clean energy”.

But it does not explicitly require that electrification be powered by renewable energy. Around one-third of global electricity is produced using coal and another fifth using fossil gas.

Attempts by Saudi Arabia, India and Kenya meanwhile to delay the next major reports by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) have been another major source of friction at the talks.

The draft text “highlights the importance” of these reports for an upcoming stocktake of global carbon-cutting efforts in 2028.

Dozens of countries across Europe, Africa and the Pacific want these assessments by the IPCC, the global authority on climate science, published in time for that crucial stocktake.

Countries have also disagreed at COP31 over how to respond to the looming breach of the 1.5C warming target set under the Paris climate accord.

The latest draft expressed “deep concern” that global warming would cross 1.5C but some countries lamented the text did not go further.

“We are profoundly disappointed by the substance of the cover decision,” said UK climate negotiator Kate Hughes.

“It moves us backwards on the science... It is a lowest common denominator where it should have been, instead, presenting bold collective ambition on climate action.”

The talks also jammed over long-running complaints that rich nations are shirking their obligations to help developing nations confront climate change.

The removal of a $120-billion target for climate adaptation angered developing nations.

“We need finance, yet our partners showed up to this COP with empty hands,” said Jetnil-Kijiner of the Marshall Islands.

“We cannot do this on our own. We cannot survive on empty promises.”

Speaking to reporters at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on Sunday evening, Nahid said the NCP had been the first to call for national unity on August 5. However, he alleged that the BNP had undermined that unity by disregarding the reform proposals and the verdict on the July Charter.
He also blamed the government's failure for the ongoing anarchy allegedly involving Awami League activists.

Addressing the country's deteriorating law and order situation, Nahid said he had repeatedly raised concerns in parliament before leaving the country, warning about the worsening situation over the past seven months.
He said a report published six months after the government took office had identified law and order as the country's most critical area of concern.
He attributed the current situation to what he described as the government's indifference.

item.title: Report: Industrial rebound drives late-FY26 growth surge
item.description:
Bangladesh’s economy closed FY26 on a note of cautious optimism, propelled by a dramatic final-quarter rebound in manufacturing that lifted annual growth even as banking-sector distress and geopolitical supply shocks continued to cloud the horizon.
According to the Bangladesh Bank Quarterly (April–June 2026), provisional real GDP growth accelerated sharply to 4.60% in the fourth quarter (Q4FY26), up from 2.22% in the preceding quarter and 2.05% a year earlier.
This late surge pushed full-year FY26 real GDP growth to 3.68% (with macroeconomic framework estimates reaching 4.14%), outpacing the 3.49% recorded in FY25.
The primary engine behind the recovery was a decisive turnaround in the industrial sector, which expanded by 6.52% in Q4FY26 after contracting by 0.28% in Q3.
Large-scale manufacturing led the charge with an 11% expansion—driven by wearing apparel, food products, chemicals, and transport equipment—while small, medium, and micro enterprises grew by 7%.
Services also gained traction, expanding 4.28% in the final quarter.
However, the recovery remained uneven: agriculture grew by a subdued 1.73% in Q4, and electricity, gas, and water supply continued to contract amid ongoing energy shortages aggravated by Middle East hostilities.
Inflation, credit squeeze, and external resilience
High non-performing loans (NPLs) and weak business confidence have severely dampened banks' appetite for risk, causing private-sector credit growth to slump to 4.47% in Q4FY26—far short of the central bank’s 8.5% target.
Consequently, banks parked surplus funds in risk-free government securities, driving excess liquidity up 108.39% year-on-year to Tk408,081 crore and fueling a 30.43% surge in public-sector credit growth.
Simultaneously, point-to-point headline inflation crept back up to 9.16% in June 2026 from 8.71% in March, driven by domestic energy tariff adjustments and global fuel price spikes linked to the US–Iran conflict.
Although bumper Boro harvests pushed rice inflation into deflationary territory (negative 3.9%), surging vegetable, fruit, and transport costs kept real wage growth negative.
To combat inflation, Bangladesh Bank held its policy rate steady at 10% throughout Q4FY26.
However, in a major post-quarter pivot effective August 2, 2026, the central bank cut the policy rate by 50 basis points to 9.50%—its first rate reduction in six years—and unveiled a Tk60,000 crore stimulus package (including revolving refinance schemes for closed industries, export diversification, green factories, and agriculture) to jumpstart private investment.
Amid domestic headwinds, the external sector stood out as a pillar of stability. Robust workers’ remittances—which rose 17.3% annually to $35.59 billion, increasingly aided by mobile financial services—combined with stronger medium- and long-term external financing to generate an overall Balance of Payments surplus of $2.93 billion in Q4FY26.
Under a market-based exchange rate regime, the Taka held steady around Tk122.75–122.85 per dollar, enabling Bangladesh Bank to purchase a net $6.43 billion from the market in FY26 and boost gross official reserves to $37.58 billion ($32.93 billion under BPM6), covering roughly 5.4 months of prospective imports.
Meanwhile, domestic capital markets staged a strong rally, with the DSEX climbing 11.29 percent in the final quarter.

item.title: Curbing tax evasion: NBR to restructure int’l tax unit
item.description:
The National Board of Revenue (NBR) is strengthening international tax management to stop illicit profit shifting and tax evasion through multinational companies (MNCs).
To this end, an initiative has been taken to restructure the agency's international tax wing.
Under this NBR initiative, the Transfer Pricing (TP) Cell, formed in 2014, is being brought under the International Tax Unit (ITU). According to NBR sources, this information has come to light.
It is learned that NBR is placing greater emphasis on international tax management as part of the government's efforts to attract foreign investment and sign Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) with various countries.
A decision has also been made to rent a separate office to strengthen the operations of the new unit.
Due to weak international tax management, Bangladesh faces the risk of losing a massive amount of revenue.
According to estimates by the Tax Justice Network (TJN), between 2016 and 2022, Bangladesh lost nearly $1.27 billion in corporate and individual income tax revenue.
Of this, corporate tax revenue losses amounted to roughly $1.2 billion.
An official speaking on condition of anonymity said work has begun. First, the new unit will review whether any amendments are needed to the Income Tax Act regarding international tax provisions, particularly transfer pricing.
The TP Cell will monitor whether profit shifting or transfer pricing is occurring not only in multinational companies, but also in cross-border transactions of domestic companies. For this, international tax rules also need to be further strengthened.
According to various NBR assessments, at least 500 foreign companies, including branch and liaison offices, are operating in Bangladesh.
These companies have also submitted Statements of International Transactions (SIT) as per the instructions of the Transfer Pricing Cell.
However, for the past three years, initiatives to enforce the transfer pricing law by properly monitoring the activities of multinational companies and collecting SITs have remained virtually stalled.
According to NBR sources, tax files of various multinational companies are currently scattered across 33 tax zones in the country.
NBR plans to bring these files under the new unit.
Although the tax files of many multinational companies are currently under the Large Taxpayers Unit (LTU), other tax zones are also handling the tax files of such companies.
On the other hand, Tax Zone-11 oversees the income tax returns and tax payment records of foreign nationals.
In addition, relevant officials stated that issuing various certificates under Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAAs), tax clearance certificates for foreign nationals traveling abroad, and necessary approvals from the tax office will be managed centrally through the new unit.
Officials said transfer pricing provisions were introduced in 2014 to prevent tax evasion through cross-border profit shifting by multinational companies.
NBR also received technical assistance from the European Union (EU) to train officials for implementing this work.
However, because many trained officials have now been transferred to different tax zones, the activities of the TP Cell have become virtually inactive.
NBR sources said a delegation from Poland is scheduled to visit Bangladesh to discuss transfer pricing matters. The delegation has also expressed interest in meeting with trained officials on the issue.
Relevant officials say that capital flight through under-invoicing and over-invoicing of goods in imports and exports, along with Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) strategies, are now major challenges for the global tax system.
To counter these strategies identified by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), it has become urgent to increase expertise and surveillance in international tax management.

item.title: Defaulters with court’s stay orders can avail Tk60,000cr stimulus
item.description:
Even if identified as a loan defaulter, customers will receive loan facilities from the stimulus fund announced by Bangladesh Bank if there is a court stay order on the relevant loan.
The central bank has taken this decision to ensure the implementation of 15 stimulus schemes worth Tk60,000 crore announced for economic recovery.
Bangladesh Bank’s Banking Regulation and Policy Department (BRPD) issued a circular in this regard recently.
The circular, sent to the managing directors and chief executive officers of all scheduled banks in the country, stated that this directive will come into effect immediately.
The central bank's circular said that if a court issues a stay order on the relevant loan following a lawsuit or writ filed by a borrower after becoming a defaulter, that customer will be considered eligible to receive loans under Bangladesh Bank's stimulus program.
However, Bangladesh Bank clarified that this new directive will apply only to the eligibility of loan defaulters who have obtained a court stay order; all other terms and conditions of the stimulus schemes will remain unchanged as before.
According to Bangladesh Bank sources, a total of 15 stimulus schemes worth Tk60,000 crore are currently active to keep economic activities dynamic, create direct and indirect employment, and maintain the competitiveness of entrepreneurs.

item.title: Minimum Wage Board meets Monday; RMG owners set to submit wage proposal
item.description:
The third meeting of the Minimum Wage Board will be held on Monday to review recommendations before determining a new wage structure for ready-made garment (RMG) workers, with factory owners expected to submit their new wage proposal at the session.
The meeting is scheduled for 11:30am at the Department of Labour in the capital, presided over by Board Chairman and Judge Syed Azad Subhani.
An earlier meeting slated for November 16 was postponed due to unavoidable circumstances, after which a notice announced the new date.
The board is expected to review opinions from worker and employer representatives along with relevant issues to move forward with drafting its minimum wage recommendations.
At its first meeting on November 4, the board instructed both sides to prepare and submit their respective wage structure proposals at the next sitting.
Subsequently, at the second meeting on November 9, worker representative Babul Akhter presented a four-grade monthly minimum wage structure for workers, proposing Tk48,000 for Grade 1, Tk43,000 for Grade 2, Tk38,000 for Grade 3, and Tk32,000 for Grade 4, alongside Tk30,000 for newly recruited or apprentice workers.
For office staff and employees, the workers' side proposed Tk55,000 in Grade 1, Tk50,000 in Grade 2, Tk45,000 in Grade 3, and Tk40,000 in Grade 4.
Employers were unable to submit their proposal at the second meeting; although they sought seven working days, the board granted four working days, setting a November 15 deadline for submission.
Currently, the minimum monthly wage for RMG workers stands at Tk12,500, which was announced in November 2023 and took effect in December that year, up from Tk8,000 set in 2018. Worker organizations have long been campaigning for a revised minimum wage—with broader demands pressing for at least Tk 30,000 a month—citing rising prices of essentials, house rent, healthcare, and overall living costs.
The government formed the six-member Minimum Wage Board on November 1, chaired by District and Sessions Judge Syed Azad Subhani, with Dhaka University Public Administration Professor Dr Mosleh Uddin Ahmed as the neutral member.
Representing employers are Bangladesh Employers’ Federation Joint Secretary General Asif Ayub and Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) Director ABM Shamsuddin, while workers are represented by Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal President Anwar Hossain and Bangladesh Garments and Industrial Workers Federation General Secretary Babul Akhter.

item.title: Debt rising, but how much the capacity to repay improving?
item.description:
The per capita foreign debt of people in Bangladesh is now approximately 646 USD, according to the World Bank's International Debt Report 2026. The report also mentioned, by the end of 2025, Bangladesh's total foreign debt stood at 113.44 billion USD. This is 8.6 per cent higher than the previous year and nearly three times the 38.77 billion USD of 2015.

A crucial question in assessing the debt-to-GDP ratio is whether the debt is being used to create opportunities to increase future income. It is also important to see if the country can repay its debt without reducing expenditure on essential sectors like education and health, and whether foreign currency earnings are sufficient to meet foreign debt obligations.

In the current economic situation of Bangladesh, these questions have become even more significant. In 2025, the country's foreign debt amounted to 23.6 per cent of the gross national income and 210.5 per cent of export earnings. During the same period, the expenditure on interest and principal repayment of foreign debts was equivalent to 15.7 per cent of export earnings. These figures indicate that sound debt management is vital for effective government financial management and foreign exchange market stability.

It is important to understand the difference between foreign debt and total government debt. The World Bank's accounting for foreign debt includes loans taken by the government, loans with government guarantees, foreign loans of the private sector without government guarantees, and short-term loans. On the other hand, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Bangladesh's total government debt in FY 2024-25 was 41.3 per cent of GDP, and more than half of this was domestic debt. Hence, these two scopes of accounting are different and should not be interpreted as the same type of debt accounting.

Bangladesh's debt-to-GDP ratio is a cause for concern because the country's economy has not yet achieved sustainable stability. Prolonged high inflation, stagnation in private investment, weaknesses in the banking sector, revenue collection shortfalls, low direct foreign investment, and risks to the export sector due to the international situation are putting pressure on the economy. In such a scenario, excessive spending on interest and principal repayment of debt can lead to a shortage of funds needed for productivity growth, job creation, and essential reforms.

One of the main reasons for the increase in Bangladesh's debt is borrowing for infrastructure development and budget deficits. If loan funds are invested in planned projects such as ports, power transmission systems, railways, or flood prevention, productivity can increase. This enhances the economy's capacity and makes debt repayment easier.

However, if project costs increase, implementation is delayed, or if expected economic benefits are not realised after project completion, problems arise. Such experiences have been observed in Bangladesh over the past decade. In these cases, the liability for debt remains, but the expected economic growth is not achieved through the utilization of that debt.

The exchange rate of the Taka poses a significant risk in the case of foreign debt. If the value of Taka declines, the cost of repaying the loan in Taka increases even if the amount borrowed in USD remains unchanged. The risk is particularly high for projects that require importing machinery from abroad but do not directly earn foreign currency. Therefore, before taking on a project, it is not enough to consider only construction costs and potential benefits within the country.

It is necessary to assess how much foreign currency will be needed for project implementation and operation and to what extent the project will contribute to export growth, import cost savings, or earning foreign currency by other means. After transitioning from the list of least developed countries, Bangladesh needs to be prepared for situations where some special financial facilities may decrease, and new loans might come with comparatively tough conditions. Therefore, it is necessary to adopt a well-planned debt management strategy from now on.

Firstly, realistic plans to increase revenue in the medium term are needed. The taxation system must be made fair and predictable by expanding the tax base. In order to achieve this, it is essential to apply digital technology in tax administration, reduce special tax exemptions, ensure compliance with laws, and simplify tax payments. The responsibility of tax policy formulation and collection must also be clearly separated.

Secondly, all government sector loans need to be managed in an integrated manner. The government must specify the amount, interest, duration, source, and annual repayment amount in its debt management strategy. Future financial liabilities from state-owned enterprises, government guarantees, and public-private partnership projects must also be disclosed.

Thirdly, to enhance efficiency and accountability in government investment, each major project's costs and potential benefits should be independently evaluated. Practical estimates for land acquisition, import, maintenance, and expenditures in foreign currency should be included. Priority should be given to projects that contribute significantly to productivity, economic risk management, and employment generation. Weak or less fruitful projects should be re-evaluated and halted if necessary.

Fourthly, after transitioning from the list of least developed countries, efforts must be made to increase foreign currency earning capacity to face changes in international trade. In 2026, Bangladesh signed economic partnership agreements with Japan in February and South Korea in August, which could create opportunities for increasing trade and investment.

However, exports will not increase just by signing agreements; to reap the benefits, businesses must meet rules of origin conditions and labour and environmental standards. Additionally, it is crucial to improve the efficiency of tariffs, ports, and transport systems.

Fifthly, reforms aimed at increasing economic growth must be aligned with debt management policies. The weaknesses in the financial sector, lack of reliable energy supply, limited competition in the market, and various barriers in business operations reduce the benefits of public and private investment. Therefore, prompt and effective measures must be taken to increase revenue collection, ensure banking sector stability, energy security, and improve the business environment.

Conducting development activities through borrowing is a conventional system. Even developed countries borrow. What is important in borrowing is to use the funds in such a way that productivity increases, the economy becomes more capable of dealing with various risks, and the conditions for debt repayment in the future align with the debt terms. The main consideration here is whether Bangladesh can create any assets in exchange for each new debt that will bring benefits to the economy, increase government revenue, or strengthen foreign currency earning capacity.

item.title: Seven health tests made mandatory for 2027 Hajj pilgrims before vaccination
item.description:
The government has made seven types of medical tests mandatory for pilgrims of the 2027 Hajj before they receive vaccinations.
The Religious Affairs Ministry issued a notice in this regard on Sunday.
According to the notice, pilgrims must undergo the tests at government hospitals at district and upazila levels or designated private hospitals across the country.
The mandatory tests include blood grouping and Rh typing, Complete Blood Count (CBC) with ESR, urine R/M/E, chest X-ray, electrocardiogram (ECG), random blood sugar (RBS) and serum creatinine.
Pilgrims suffering from chronic or serious illnesses may need additional medical examinations depending on their health conditions, it said.
For suspected heart failure, echocardiography will be required.
Pilgrims with kidney complications may need serum creatinine, ultrasonography of the kidneys and urinary bladder, and serum urea tests.
Those suspected of having liver complications will have to undergo serum bilirubin, SGPT, albumin-globulin ratio, whole-abdomen ultrasonography, upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy and prothrombin time tests.
For the detection of chronic lung diseases, sputum for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) testing and chest CT scans may be required, said the notice.
In cases involving pregnancy-related complications, a urine pregnancy test during the first three months and an ultrasonography under a pregnancy profile will be necessary.
Pilgrims must submit copies of their medical test reports and e-health profiles to the medical team at designated vaccination centres before receiving their vaccines.
A health certificate will be issued to pilgrims after they complete the vaccination process.
For information and assistance regarding Hajj, prospective pilgrims have been advised to contact the Hajj Call Centre at 16136.

item.title: Rooppur's first unit begins second grid-integration test
item.description:
The country's first nuclear power plant, Rooppur, resumed trial electricity supply to the national grid for the second time on Monday morning.
The first unit began supplying power at 10:20am, with output expected to range between 300MW and 350MW.
Project Director Dr Md Kabir Hossain said the second phase of the trial would continue for 10 to 24 hours. During this period, engineers will assess the plant's generation performance and the effectiveness of its coordination with the national grid.
Rooppur first began trial power supply to the grid on November 17. After being connected at 3:16pm, the first unit's output reached a maximum of 350MW. The initial test run lasted around eight and a half hours, ending at 11:50pm, when the plant was disconnected from the grid for technical assessment.
During the first phase, engineers monitored the performance and stability of the plant's turbine, generator and grid connection systems. The second phase will further assess the equipment and the plant's ability to synchronise power supply with the national grid.
Located in Ishwardi, Pabna, the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has two units, each with a generation capacity of 1,200MW. Once both units become fully operational, the plant will have a combined capacity of 2,400MW.
However, the start of trial electricity supply does not mean commercial production has begun. The plant must complete several stages of technical testing and performance assessments and secure the necessary regulatory approvals before moving to commercial operation.

item.title: Global dengue cases rise 34-fold in three decades
item.description:
Reported dengue cases worldwide have increased 34-fold over the past three decades, with South Asia among the regions experiencing the fastest growth, according to a new international study highlighting the disease's expanding geographical reach.
Presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene on Sunday in National Harbor, Maryland, the study estimates that 74 million dengue cases were reported across 143 countries between 1990 and 2024.
Of these, 10.7 million cases were missing from existing World Health Organization (WHO) databases, suggesting that global surveillance records have substantially underestimated reported infections.
The findings are particularly significant for Bangladesh, which is facing another major dengue outbreak.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), 173,473 patients have been hospitalized and 518 have died from dengue between January 1 and Sunday this year.
In the 24 hours until 8am on Sunday, two more people died and 1,519 patients were admitted to hospitals nationwide. Dhaka Division recorded the highest number of new admissions, at 755.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune, Dr Ahyoung Lim, the study's lead researcher from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), said South Asia was among the regions experiencing the fastest growth in reported dengue incidence.
The increase was particularly rapid in regions where dengue has emerged more recently, including Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, compared with some regions where the disease has been endemic for longer.
However, the study does not explain the sharp rise in reported cases.
Lim said climate, urbanisation and international travel are commonly considered important factors in dengue transmission, but the research did not examine their individual contributions.
“The faster growth in Africa, the Middle East and South Asia is likely to be due to both real spread and to improved recognition and diagnosis in countries which only very recently have been reporting dengue,” he said.
This distinction matters because rising reported cases may reflect both an actual expansion of dengue transmission and better detection and surveillance.
Bangladesh has experienced increasingly severe dengue outbreaks in recent years, with 2023 marking the worst on record.
DGHS recorded 321,179 hospitalizations and 1,705 deaths in 2023, followed by 101,214 hospitalizations and 575 deaths in 2024, and 102,861 hospitalisations and 413 deaths in 2025.
The 2026 outbreak has already surpassed the number of hospitalizations recorded in either of the previous two years, with more than 173,000 patients admitted by November 22.
The new study offers a broader picture of dengue trends by reconstructing historical estimates for periods and locations where surveillance data were incomplete.
Lim said the research team had made its country-level estimates publicly available, including monthly and annual figures with corresponding uncertainty intervals.
The dataset includes Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka, allowing researchers to examine historical trends in reported dengue cases across South Asia.
However, the researchers did not rank individual countries by incidence or growth, noting that differences in surveillance and reporting could affect comparisons.
“Our paper is about global and regional trends and doesn't involve any country rankings,” Lim said.
He added that variations between countries could reflect differences in surveillance and reporting rather than actual differences in dengue transmission.
Dengue is primarily transmitted by infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which thrive in urban areas where stagnant water provides breeding sites.
Temperature, rainfall and humidity influence mosquito survival, breeding patterns and the potential for virus transmission. Rapid urbanisation, population movement and international travel can also contribute to the geographical spread of dengue.
Lim said these factors were relevant to emerging hotspots such as Bangladesh, although the study did not assess their individual contributions.
“Temperature, rainfall and urbanisation are all known to impact the mosquitoes that carry dengue and are often regarded as key factors in the emergence of hotspots such as Bangladesh,” he said.
He added that the study's estimates could provide a foundation for further research into the environmental and human factors shaping dengue transmission.
The research also highlights the importance of strengthening disease surveillance, particularly in countries where limited diagnostic capacity and inconsistent reporting may obscure the actual scale of outbreaks.

item.title: Bangladesh tops EU list for irregular migration
item.description:
Bangladesh has ranked first among countries for irregular entry into the European Union (EU) for two consecutive years, EU Ambassador to Bangladesh Michael Miller has said.
The issue is set to feature as the only country-specific agenda item at a meeting of interior ministers from all 27 EU member states in early December.
Miller also expressed surprise and described as “unacceptable” the recruitment of Bangladeshi nationals to fight on the front lines of Russia's war in Ukraine.
He made the remarks at a DCAB Talk organised at the National Press Club on Monday.
Alongside concerns over irregular migration, the ambassador outlined a broader framework for strengthening Bangladesh-EU relations, covering trade, investment, infrastructure development, a potential free trade agreement (FTA) and the Rohingya crisis.
Miller said Bangladesh had ranked first in terms of irregular border crossings and entries into the EU over the past two years.
He said many Bangladeshis fell victim to human traffickers and brokers while attempting to reach Europe through irregular routes. Some intermediaries misuse Umrah visas or encourage migrants to overstay their work contracts, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation and extortion.
The ambassador stressed the need for stricter regulation of brokers and intermediaries and action against unscrupulous recruiting agencies.
He also highlighted initiatives to expand safe and legal migration pathways, improve skills development and facilitate discussions in Dhaka in January on an operational arrangement with Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency.
Describing the EU as Bangladesh's largest export destination and a major trading partner, Miller said nearly half of the country's total exports went to the EU market, amounting to 23.3 billion euros in 2025.
The 25th anniversary of the EU's Everything But Arms (EBA) scheme was also recently celebrated.
He said the EU had voted in favour of extending the preparatory period for Bangladesh's graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category to ensure a smooth and predictable transition.
However, he stressed that the additional time must be used to implement realistic and measurable domestic reforms, strengthen oversight and ensure an effective role for the private sector.
On a potential FTA, Miller said the EU was conducting a scoping exercise and had invited Bangladesh to the first round of direct discussions in December.
He said any agreement would need to ensure balanced commitments and reciprocal market access, adding that labour rights, environmental protection and good governance would remain central to bilateral relations.
Miller said the EU viewed Bangladesh as an equal partner, moving beyond the traditional donor-recipient relationship.
Highlighting major projects under the EU's Global Gateway initiative, he mentioned an ongoing initiative with Airbus to modernise Bangladesh's aircraft fleet, investment in the development of the Laldia Green Container Terminal at Chittagong Port, and financing for the country's first electrified railway line.
The railway project was recently approved by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec).
Although the EU has been the leading source of foreign direct investment (FDI) in Bangladesh over the past two years, Miller said the current level of investment remained below its potential.
To attract more investment, the EU, in collaboration with Invest Bangladesh, will organise its first Business and Investment Forum in Dhaka on April 5-6 next year.
The forum will focus on circularity in the ready-made garment (RMG) sector, leather, agribusiness, logistics and connectivity.
Miller stressed that policy predictability, transparency, enforcement of contracts and the effective functioning of commercial courts were essential to attracting foreign investment.
Referring to the 2017 atrocities in Myanmar and last week's ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), Miller said the EU had stood by Bangladesh since the beginning of the Rohingya crisis, providing more than half a billion euros in humanitarian assistance.
He said the EU had allocated 31.5 million euros in humanitarian assistance for 2026, while development projects worth 50 million euros were underway in Cox's Bazar to support both the local population and Rohingya refugees.
Reaffirming the EU's support for the safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya, Miller said the bloc looked forward to Bangladesh's formulation of a new strategy on the crisis.

item.title: Democrats win largest US House majority since 1992
item.description:
Democrats have won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives in more than three decades, after Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina, US media projected on Sunday.
The party won full control of both the House and Senate in a sweeping midterm rout with a landslide of upsets that delivered a crushing rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.
CBS News and NBC News projected Hubbard’s win on Sunday, securing the Democrats a 258th seat in Congress’ 435-member House.
The majority is the largest won by either party since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.
It also beats the 257 seats won when Barack Obama was elected president in 2008 but falls short of the 334-seat majority the party won at the end of the 1930s, which is the largest on record.
Republicans have not controlled more than 250 House seats since the start of the Great Depression which saw mass unemployment, acute deflation and widespread poverty.
“House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM,” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a post on X.
The 56-year-old New Yorker is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House, after being nominated by his party.
Sunday’s result came after Foxx requested a recount.
Hubbard said Sunday that he had spoken with Foxx, who “graciously conceded following the results of the recount process.”
“Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices,” he added on X.
Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, won election to the Senate, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate from North Carolina since 2008.
Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.
The Democrats midterm triumph hands the party the power to block Trump’s agenda and investigate alleged corruption for the last two years of his presidency.
Democrats have already unveiled plans for wide-ranging investigations into Trump officials and his business interests when they take control of the lower chamber in January.
Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, sent 12 letters on Wednesday, warning members of Trump’s family and senior administration figures to preserve documents ahead of investigations into alleged corruption, immigration abuses and the handling of files related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The administration has pushed back against the threatened scrutiny.
November’s midterm results reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump’s war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.

item.title: Iran says will use ‘all available means’ to counter US blockade
item.description:
Iran said Monday it would use all means at its disposal to counter a US naval blockade that was imposed in retaliation for its own push to block the Strait of Hormuz.
“We will certainly not tolerate these actions and will use all available means to counter US aggression,” said foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing.
War broke out between Iran and the United States on February 28 when US-Israeli strikes killed the Islamic republic’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
The conflict has since expanded after Iran retaliated with missile and drone strikes across the region and with militant groups it backs in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq also entering the fray.
The Strait of Hormuz has become the focus of the conflict, with Iran continuing in its efforts to blockade the waterway, vital to global energy supplies.
In response, the US imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports. It later announced a raft of economic sanctions, and launched a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran.
“You should bear in mind that what the Americans have described as economic sanctions, an economic blockade and a naval blockade undoubtedly constitutes an act of military aggression against Iran,” said Baqaei.
“Under these circumstances, Iran is entitled, pursuant to Article 51 of the UN Charter, to use any means at its disposal to defend itself.”
Iranian forces have made multiple announcements in recent weeks of ships catching fire attempting to use routes that Tehran considers off-limits.
Diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June deal that laid out a pathway to a permanent settlement.
Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days but only if Washington agreed to its list of demands which include the lifting of the blockade.
“If the American side fulfils its commitments, security can be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the region in the shortest possible time,” said Baqaei.
